routes.description: Establish that historically meaningful witness traces survived in the Gospel and resurrection traditions despite ordinary discrepancies, transmission, and theological interpretation, and that the total attestation warrants confidence beyond a purely visionary or literary origin.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source proximity and retained local knowledge support substantial continuity, that discrepancies and unusual narrative features are compatible with sincere witness-derived transmission, and that the resurrection evidence resists the proposed ordinary causal alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The combined documentary and resurrection evidence must justify substantial historical confidence in witness-derived traditions without requiring complete inerrancy.

centralBridges.description: Establish sufficient chronological, geographical, and cultural continuity between the narrated events and the surviving accounts.
Explain why contradictions and variations can arise within broadly truthful, independently transmitted testimony.
Show that the resurrection traditions’ content and effects are inadequately explained by ordinary visions or later apologetic construction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify how the quantity and independence of early attestation should affect confidence in extraordinary claims.
Account for doubt, misrecognition, physicality, and other resistant details as potential traces of unusual experiences.

routes.description: Establish that ordinary historical analysis supports only a limited reconstruction of Jesus and the rise of resurrection belief because the Gospels are late, dependent, anonymous, internally divergent, and shaped by oral transmission and theological controversy.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source relationships and contradictions limit independence and straightforward reliability, that historical method cannot privilege unprecedented supernatural explanations over familiar alternatives, and that visions plus theological reinterpretation explain resurrection belief and its narrative development.

motionBridge.description: The surviving evidence must support only bounded historical claims while leaving bodily resurrection historically unestablished.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate how dependence, authorship, dating, transmission, and contradiction constrain the Gospels’ evidentiary independence and accuracy.
Apply comparative historical probability to miracle reports without assuming either their impossibility or their occurrence.
Provide an ordinary causal account connecting post-crucifixion experiences, messianic reinterpretation, and emerging resurrection belief.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate well-supported baseline claims such as Jesus’s existence from less secure claims about particular deeds and sayings.
Explain difficult resurrection details through the narratives’ literary, theological, and polemical functions.

sections.title: Documentary Base, Dating, and Historical Proximity
sections.rationale: The identity, relationships, dating, and local knowledge of the surviving sources determine how closely their traditions can be connected to eyewitnesses and the events they narrate.

sections.title: Transmission, Variation, and Gospel Contradictions
sections.rationale: The debate must determine whether differences among the accounts are compatible with broadly truthful transmission or instead demonstrate alteration that materially limits historical confidence.

sections.title: Historical Method and Extraordinary Claims
sections.rationale: The standard used to compare miracle reports with ordinary alternative explanations governs whether strong attestation could ever support a resurrection or other unprecedented event.

sections.title: Experiences and the Origins of Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: Competing explanations of visions, messianic reinterpretation, missionary action, and the emergence of Christian belief bear directly on whether a bodily resurrection is required by the evidence.

sections.title: Resurrection Narratives: Witness Traces or Apologetic Development
sections.rationale: Doubt, misrecognition, empty-tomb material, physical demonstrations, and supernatural features must be assessed as either resistant experiential traces or products of later literary and theological debate.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Mark was probably written first and used by Matthew and Luke, while John substantially differs from the Synoptics in its miracles, encounters, teachings, and extended speeches.
moves.attributionBasis: The guest explicitly labels the account as his view and the common scholarly view, then gives a sustained comparison of the four Gospels.

response.rationale: This is a constructive source-critical argument and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops a central source-critical distinction with concrete comparisons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim distinguishes probable Synoptic dependence from substantial Johannine difference without conflating them.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic wording matches the textual similarities offered, while Johannine difference is illustrated rather than absolutized.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from extensive shared sequence and wording to literary dependence is clear, with Johannine distinctiveness separately supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific textual relationships and categories of Johannine difference support the claim, though representative passages are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It sits at the top of the central tier because source dependence and distinctiveness directly constrain evidentiary independence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily presents a positive source comparison rather than engaging a developed competing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Markan priority, shared sequence and wording in Matthew and Luke, and separate Synoptic classification; the locked proposition records the sustained Johannine comparison.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Paul’s early report of meeting James strongly supports Jesus’s historical existence, but that baseline does not establish what Jesus said or did.
moves.attributionBasis: The guest answers the interviewer’s mythicism question, states his historical method, and supplies Paul’s meeting with James as a concrete reason.

response.rationale: This is a constructive calibrated-baseline move and has no earlier opposing locked move requiring response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a concrete historical datum and expressly limits what that datum establishes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The existence conclusion and its sharp limitation regarding deeds and sayings are both expressly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Strong confidence in existence is tied to Paul’s meeting with James, while the move explicitly denies broader historical entailments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidence supports the narrow existence baseline, and the conclusion carefully blocks an invalid extension to sayings or deeds.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul’s reported contact with James is a specific early datum, although alternative readings of the kinship designation are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly occupies the subsidiary tier by separating a well-supported existence baseline from more contested biographical claims.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is assessed; the move instead marks the limited reach of its own evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Paul’s meetings with James, identified as Jesus’s brother, and immediately states that existence does not establish what Jesus said or did.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The Gospels preserve some credible history but cannot be read straightforwardly because they contradict one another, were anonymously written decades later by non-eyewitnesses, and transmit changing oral stories.
moves.attributionBasis: The guest directly answers why proximity does not make the narratives wholly credible and gives an extended, enumerated explanation of contradictions, authorship, and oral transmission.

response.rationale: This source-transmission case is constructive in the locked inventory and therefore carries no reply target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies several mutually reinforcing reasons for limiting straightforward historical use.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition preserves some credible history while precisely identifying anonymity, delay, non-eyewitness authorship, contradiction, and oral change.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The qualified conclusion that straightforward reading is unwarranted fits the enumerated transmission limitations without claiming total unreliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The multiple source limitations coherently support bounded confidence, although the bridge from oral transmission to actual alteration is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Authorship posture, language, dating, and transmission are specifically identified, but the frequency and direction of oral change receive limited documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is nearly maximal central-tier contact because it directly addresses authorship, dating, transmission, contradiction, and evidentiary accuracy.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops affirmative transmission criticism without expressly testing a particular continuity-based alternative account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes third-person narration, no eyewitness claim, a different language, decades of distance, and the unresolved route by which stories reached the authors.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: Historians must explain whether miraculous content itself supplies an additional reason to distrust a story when its transmission history otherwise matches that of a non-miraculous story.
moves.attributionBasis: The interviewer explicitly poses a controlled comparison after agreeing that history is skeptical, developing it through matched stories that differ only in miraculous content.

components.text: Whether the stated transmission defects justify extra distrust when two otherwise matched stories differ only by miraculous content.

response.rationale: The controlled comparison contacts the inference from transmission defects to distrust and asks whether miracle content independently changes the historical assessment, but it does not defeat the documented defects themselves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer because it contacts the decisive inferential standard while leaving the underlying source-critical premises intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The matched-story hypothetical clearly isolates miraculous content as the variable whose evidentiary effect requires explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As an explicitly framed methodological question, its force is appropriately limited and does not presume the answer.

charity.alternative: Transmission defects can reduce confidence in both stories even if miracle content creates an additional base-rate concern.
charity.decisiveQualification: The controlled comparison isolates only the additional effect of miraculous content, not the independent force of transmission defects.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Holding transmission history constant is a clean controlled comparison that exposes the disputed role of prior plausibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hypothetical effectively identifies a methodological burden, but it supplies no empirical base-rate or concrete attestation comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central historical-method bridge by asking whether miraculous content is being treated as independently disqualifying.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly preserves the skeptical transmission premises while pressing a distinct and legitimate methodological question.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly matches lateness, oral history, and language, then varies only whether the story contains a miracle.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historians cannot establish an unprecedented miracle merely from transmitted reports when invention or alteration provides a more historically probable explanation, although this does not declare the miracle impossible.
moves.attributionBasis: The guest answers the interviewer’s controlled comparison continuously, invokes general historical criteria and an analogous miracle worker, and states the probabilistic conclusion.

components.text: Whether miraculous content supplies an additional historical reason for distrust when transmission histories are otherwise matched.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers that historians compare the unprecedented event with invention or alteration and seek what probably happened, while expressly avoiding a claim of impossibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a full answer with explicit contact to the methodological comparison and a stated probabilistic consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between historical establishment and metaphysical possibility is explicit and stable throughout the argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion concerns comparative historical probability, not impossibility, and the qualification materially constrains the claim.

charity.alternative: Matched transmission histories could permit strong evidence to overcome a miracle’s initially low historical probability.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must compare actual evidentiary strength with invention or alteration rather than treating unprecedented content as impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative-probability framework is coherent, but the move compresses the bridge from unprecedented character to the superiority of alteration or invention.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: General historical practice and an analogous miracle worker provide support, but relevant base rates and evidentiary thresholds remain largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is near the top of the central tier because it directly states the method governing historical treatment of miracle reports.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes probabilistic comparison and disclaims impossibility, though the actual threshold at which evidence could overcome alternatives remains underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how walking on water could be historically established, invokes ordinary historical probability, and the locked proposition preserves the explicit non-impossibility qualification.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: A sufficiently large and independent body of testimony, including witnesses disposed toward skepticism, should be capable of increasing the historical probability assigned to an apparent miracle.
moves.attributionBasis: The questioning explicitly develops Douthat’s challenge through the example of well-attested reports of levitating saints.

components.text: Whether sufficiently numerous, independent, and skeptical witnesses can raise a miracle report’s historical probability despite its low prior frequency.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges any fixed evidentiary ceiling by specifying independence, multiplicity, and skeptical witnesses, although it does not demonstrate that the resurrection evidence has those properties.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive methodological component but remains a partial answer because the hypothetical threshold is not connected to the actual record.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly conditional on a sufficiently large and independent testimonial body, with skeptical disposition specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The question asks only whether such attestation can increase probability, a modest force well matched to the hypothetical.

charity.alternative: Rare-event testimony can increase probability while still leaving ordinary error or invention more probable overall.
charity.decisiveQualification: An increase in probability does not by itself establish that the miracle probably occurred.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference that independent, reluctant testimony can provide positive likelihood evidence is clear and carefully framed as probability increase.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The specified testimonial features are relevant, but their independence and reliability are hypothetical rather than established for a concrete case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central historical-method bridge by denying that low ordinary frequency makes testimonial evidence evidentially inert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly asks for probability updating rather than declaring that testimonial quantity automatically establishes the event.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names independent witnesses, numerous writers, and people disposed toward skepticism, then asks whether any attestation level can make a miracle more probable.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historians should compare every proposed miracle with familiar alternative explanations and report only what the surviving evidence probably establishes.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman answers the attestation challenge directly and supplies an extended thermodynamic coffee example to explain probabilistic historical judgment.

components.text: How testimonial evidence should be compared with ordinary explanations when assessing whether a miracle probably occurred.
Whether historians categorically reject miraculous content or instead apply comparative probability.

response.rationale: The reply answers both challenges by requiring comparison with witness error or invention and expressly rejecting categorical impossibility, though it does not quantify how attestation changes probability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a full methodological answer with explicit comparison and qualification, missing only a developed account of testimonial updating.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently distinguishes what occurred from what surviving evidence can establish as probable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It expressly avoids categorical exclusion and limits historical conclusions to comparative probability on surviving evidence.

charity.alternative: Strong independent testimony may substantially raise the posterior probability of an extraordinary event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The raised probability still must be compared with concrete risks of error, dependence, and invention.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between past reality and historically establishable probability is explicit, consistent, and directly resolves the categorical-exclusion concern.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparative framework and error alternatives are concrete, although the coffee illustration cannot by itself establish historical base rates.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximizes central-tier relevance by articulating the governing comparative standard for extraordinary historical claims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the evidentiary relevance of testimony while insisting on comparative assessment of ordinary alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt requires comparison with witness error and fabrication, rejects categorical impossibility, and distinguishes what happened from what evidence probably establishes.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: Acts’ abrupt ending while Paul is still alive in Rome supports composition in the early 60s, which would place Luke-Acts closer to the narrated events.
moves.attributionBasis: Douthat develops the argument from the narrative endpoint of Acts and contrasts it with the momentous events omitted from the following decade.

components.text: Whether Luke-Acts must be treated as a decades-late product remote from the narrated events.

response.rationale: The move contacts the dating component by inferring an early-60s composition from Acts’ endpoint, but it does not answer anonymity, non-eyewitness authorship, oral change, or contradiction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong partial answer because it directly contests one decisive dating premise while leaving the other transmission components untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dating inference is clear, though alternative literary reasons for the ending are only implicitly excluded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The ending supports an early date, but treating authorial ignorance as the most straightforward explanation omits live narrative-purpose alternatives.

charity.alternative: Acts may end with Paul preaching in Rome for thematic or literary reasons despite later composition.
charity.decisiveQualification: An omitted later event supports early dating only if literary closure and selective narrative scope are comparatively less plausible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible but relies on the material bridge that a later author would probably have narrated Paul’s death and subsequent events.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The abrupt endpoint and omitted major events are specific evidence, but the rival explanation of deliberate literary closure is not tested.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly occupies the central source-continuity tier by directly advancing a substantially earlier date for Luke-Acts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notes the striking omitted decade but does not seriously compare the strongest literary explanation of the chosen endpoint.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies persecution, the Jewish War, and the temple’s destruction as omitted major events, then infers that the writer ended near his own chronological horizon.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Concrete contradictions among the Gospels show that authors changed inherited material and prevent treating every account as simultaneously inerrant.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman gives sustained examples involving whether disciples should carry a staff and the different Gospel chronologies of Jesus’s final Passover.

response.rationale: This is a constructive contradiction argument in the locked inventory and therefore has no earlier opposing reply target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies concrete examples and states their source-critical consequence with useful specificity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is expressly limited to simultaneous inerrancy and inherited-material change, not wholesale historical worthlessness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Genuine mutually incompatible details necessarily defeat simultaneous inerrancy, while the broader historical conclusion remains qualified.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the cited accounts are mutually incompatible, the conclusion that they cannot all be inerrant follows directly and narrowly.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The sustained staff and Passover-chronology examples are concrete and representative, though detailed harmonizations are not evaluated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is near-maximal central source-critical contact because actual contradictions directly constrain accuracy and literary independence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents contradictions constructively without developing or evaluating a particular harmonizing interpretation in the selected span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked source span contains sustained examples concerning the disciples’ staff and incompatible final-Passover chronologies, followed by the express inerrancy consequence.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: Ordinary errors, compression, and differing interpretations among related accounts are compatible with sincere eyewitness-derived transmission and do not make those accounts historically worthless.
moves.attributionBasis: Douthat uses his own memoirs and his wife’s differing account of shared experiences to model fallible but historically usable testimony.

components.text: Whether contradictions and changed details necessarily make the accounts historically worthless or incompatible with witness-derived transmission.
Whether mediated and fallible transmission can nevertheless preserve historically usable witness material.

response.rationale: The move concedes that discrepancies defeat strict inerrancy but directly argues that ordinary error and mediation remain compatible with usable testimony; it does not reconcile the concrete contradictions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive historical-worth consequence but only partially answers because it does not test whether the actual variations exceed ordinary testimonial error.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between inerrancy and historically usable eyewitness-derived mediation is clear and repeatedly maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims compatibility rather than proof of eyewitness origin and openly concedes ordinary errors and compression.

charity.alternative: Some contradictions may reflect substantive theological alteration rather than ordinary testimonial variation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing compatibility with testimony does not establish that the actual Gospel differences arose from sincere eyewitness mediation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between fallibility and historical worth is sound, with one bounded bridge from personal memoir variation to ancient mediated accounts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The memoir analogy concretely demonstrates compatible variation, but its representativeness for the Gospels’ composition and dependence is underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximizes central-tier relevance by directly explaining why contradiction need not defeat broadly witness-derived transmission.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes contradiction and inerrancy loss, though its memoir analogy only partly engages systematic literary alteration.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly separates strict inerrancy from evaluation of texts arising from eyewitnesses through mediation and permits names, dates, and details to be wrong.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: The Gospels’ accurate Palestinian geography and period-appropriate personal names indicate that substantial local knowledge survived transmission and therefore merit historical credit.
moves.attributionBasis: Douthat accurately frames Peter Williams’s argument and develops why geographical and naming accuracy bears on claims of remote, error-prone transmission.

components.text: Whether decades of remote oral transmission should have erased or corrupted Palestinian geography and period-appropriate naming knowledge.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the expected-error implication of remote transmission using retained geography and names, but it does not answer anonymity, dependence, contradiction, or accuracy of sayings.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong partial answer because it contacts continuity evidence while leaving several independent source-critical demands unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Local knowledge and continuity are recoverable, but the move slides somewhat from absence of massive geographic error to broader historical credit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Accurate local details support continuity, but the implication for narrative or sayings accuracy needs an explicit domain-specific limitation.

charity.alternative: Accurate geography and names can be preserved or researched while sayings and episodes are substantially altered.
charity.decisiveQualification: Local knowledge supports cultural continuity but does not independently establish eyewitness authorship or event-level accuracy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expected-error challenge is coherent, but the bridge from retained local knowledge to broad historical merit remains materially incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Geography and naming patterns are relevant specific categories, though the excerpt mainly invokes them through questions and cited authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the central source-continuity bridge by supplying geographical and cultural retention as evidence against total remoteness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes that alleged errors concern different material, yet it underdevelops the strongest domain-separation response.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why long transmission did not generate wrong names or massive geographical errors and contrasts retained Jericho-Jerusalem knowledge with disputed sayings.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Some followers’ post-crucifixion visions explain their belief that Jesus had been raised, while the historical evidence does not establish a bodily resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman gives a continuous first-person historical reconstruction from the disciples’ messianic expectations through claimed visions by specific followers.

response.rationale: This is the constructive statement of the ordinary causal reconstruction and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides a clear causal starting point and carefully distinguishes belief formation from bodily resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly limits the number and grouping of visions and separates followers’ belief from historical establishment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reconstruction uses expressly uncertain language about how many people experienced visions and whether groups were involved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Visions coherently explain initial conviction and persuasion, though the bridge to the full content and durability of resurrection belief is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Early belief and claimed appearances support the reconstruction, but the number, independence, and phenomenology of experiences remain uncertain.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is near-maximal central-tier contact because it supplies the initial ordinary cause in the resurrection-belief reconstruction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies a positive reconstruction without directly evaluating a developed bodily-resurrection alternative in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that some disciples believed Jesus raised, suggests some thought they saw him alive, acknowledges uncertainty about numbers and groups, and describes persuasion of others.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The empty-tomb passages may be emotionally powerful, but within the narratives the empty tomb produces doubt rather than faith and does not itself verify resurrection historically.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer directly rejects Douthat’s appeal to the human realism of the narrative and then presents Ehrman’s historical observation.

components.text: Whether retained Palestinian geography and naming patterns support continuity and historical credit for Gospel traditions.

response.rationale: The move bears on Gospel historical confidence but does not contact the local-knowledge evidence or its continuity inference; it instead argues that literary power and doubt do not verify resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant contrary material within the class but leaves the selected earlier move’s decisive local-knowledge demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely distinguishes emotional force, narrative effects of the empty tomb, and independent historical verification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that the empty tomb never produces faith is categorical within the texts and would require fuller textual demonstration, though the historical limitation is soundly qualified.

charity.alternative: Narrated doubt can itself be a realistic feature and need not show that the empty tomb lacked evidentiary significance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Psychological realism does not independently establish that the narrated empty tomb occurred historically.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference that narrative power and internal doubt do not establish historical occurrence is clear and avoids a stronger nonexistence conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The narrative observation is specific, but the universal claim across New Testament empty-tomb material is not fully documented in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly occupies the subsidiary literary-development tier by interpreting doubt and empty-tomb function rather than directly completing the natural reconstruction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response acknowledges the passages’ power while correctly separating that feature from historical verification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes the passages’ emotional power, denies that power proves occurrence, and states that the empty tomb produces doubt rather than faith within the narratives.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: Recurring doubt in the resurrection accounts is a psychologically natural response to an unprecedented bodily return and therefore need not undermine the narratives’ realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The question explicitly invokes Ehrman’s earlier premise about ordinary mortality and develops Douthat’s contrasting interpretation of doubt.

components.text: Whether recurring doubt should count against narrative realism or can be the natural response to an unprecedented bodily return.

response.rationale: The move directly reinterprets doubt as psychologically expected given the agreed rarity of resurrection, but it does not answer the separate point that doubt cannot verify the empty tomb historically.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary interpretive component but leaves the decisive historical-verification limitation substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The psychological compatibility claim is clear, although its limited evidentiary significance is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers doubt as a natural reaction rather than treating it as proof that resurrection occurred.

charity.alternative: Doubt may be psychologically realistic while still failing to verify either the empty tomb or resurrection historically.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility with realism is not positive evidence of occurrence without an additional authenticity warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given the shared premise that people do not normally rise, surprise and demands for touch are a coherent predicted reaction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Doubting Thomas example fits the psychological claim, but no comparative evidence shows this detail is more likely experiential than literary.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary narrative-strangeness bridge by giving doubt a plausible experiential interpretation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly answers the psychological reading but does not erase the opponent’s independent verification distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The short excerpt explicitly invokes the rarity of resurrection and identifies doubt and a request for physical touch as the normal human response.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: Ordinary bereavement visions do not adequately explain the early Christian combination of radical bodily-resurrection claims, persistent doubt, missionary action, and the emergence of a new religion.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person objection contrasts Ehrman’s psychological analogy with the distinctive consequences attributed to the earliest Christians.

components.text: Whether ordinary bereavement visions adequately explain the distinctive content, doubt, collective consequences, and religious movement attributed to the earliest Christians.
Whether doubt is better treated as a realistic feature than simply as failure of resurrection evidence.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges explanatory sufficiency by identifying allegedly distinctive outputs, though it does not independently establish their timing, independence, or incompatibility with social amplification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive causal demand but remains partial because the cited consequences are asserted rather than comparatively modeled.

precisionFindings.rationale: The insufficiency claim is clear, but ordinary visions, radical claims, and the emergence of a religion encompass partly unspecified causal scopes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the objection as an apparent explanatory mismatch rather than claiming that visions are impossible.

charity.alternative: A few visions combined with prior commitment, persuasion, group dynamics, and reinterpretation could generate broader belief and missionary action.
charity.decisiveQualification: The vision hypothesis need not claim that every follower independently experienced the same event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mismatch challenge is relevant, but it leaves a material bridge from unusual consequences to the inadequacy of multi-stage social explanations.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Radical claims, doubt, and movement formation are specific explananda, yet their earliest form and causal dependence are not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central natural-reconstruction bridge by challenging whether visions can explain the movement’s distinctive outputs.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presses real explanatory outputs but describes the rival too narrowly as ordinary visions followed simply by deciding they were real.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts commonplace bereavement visions with radical claims, persistent doubt, and the sudden setting in motion of a new religion.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Preexisting messianic commitment and post-crucifixion visions prompted followers to reinterpret Jesus’s death as divinely intended, salvific, and vindicated by resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman explicitly announces an explanation and gives a continuous causal reconstruction using the disciples’ prior messianic expectations.

components.text: How visions could combine with prior messianic commitment to yield salvific reinterpretation and a durable resurrection movement.

response.rationale: The reply directly supplies the missing causal mechanism: prior messianic expectation, visions, reinterpretation of defeat, divine intention, vindication, and salvation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a full answer that explicitly contacts the explanatory-sufficiency challenge and states a multi-stage causal consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal sequence and theological reinterpretation are clear, though the move implicitly generalizes from some visionaries to the follower group.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reconstruction is offered as a coherent historical explanation, with one implicit caveat regarding how broadly each stage was shared.

charity.alternative: The movement’s radical bodily claims and doubts may require more than ordinary visions and post hoc reinterpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A natural reconstruction must explain doctrinal transformation and collective spread, not merely the first reported experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The sequence from failed expectation through visions to revised divine purpose is explicit and resolves the main missing-mechanism challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Known messianic commitment and resurrection belief support the reconstruction, but the precise psychological sequence remains inferential.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximizes central-tier relevance by connecting experiences, messianic reinterpretation, salvation, and resurrection belief causally.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response squarely adds prior commitment and a detailed reinterpretive chain to answer the strongest version of the insufficiency objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt traces expectations of Roman defeat, subsequent visions, acknowledgment of misunderstanding, divine intention in Jesus’s death, resurrection vindication, and salvific reinterpretation.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The fish-eating and wound-touching scenes answer later Christians who favored spiritual resurrection and align the accounts with Jewish expectations of bodily resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The response identifies a later intra-Christian dispute and consistently attributes the physical details to the authors’ argumentative purpose.

components.text: Whether physical-touch and bodily-demonstration details are best treated as natural experiential reactions or later argumentative constructions.
Whether radical bodily content requires an original bodily event rather than later intra-Christian development.

response.rationale: The move directly offers a rival literary and polemical explanation for touch and eating scenes, although it does not specifically explain the persistence of doubt.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive authenticity inference but remains partial because doubt and the full narrative mixture are not yet addressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The identified scenes, opposing spiritual view, and bodily-resurrection purpose remain stable, with authorship of the intention implicitly inferred.
